title: Bacterial Spot of Bell Pepper (Capsicum)
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Horticultural Research (IIHR), Bengaluru & TNAU Agritech Portal
disease: Bacterial Spot (*Xanthomonas euvesicatoria* / *Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria*)
reference: ICAR Package of Practices for Vegetable Crops; TNAU Plant Pathology Crop Protection Compendium
heading: Symptoms
content: Small, water-soaked, circular to irregular lesions appear primarily on the underside of leaves. As the lesions expand, they turn dark brown to black with a greasy or water-soaked border and may develop yellow halos. Leaf spots lead to severe chlorosis and extensive premature defoliation. On fruit, raised blister-like or scabby brown spots occur.

title: Bacterial Spot of Bell Pepper (Capsicum)
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Horticultural Research (IIHR), Bengaluru & TNAU Agritech Portal
disease: Bacterial Spot (*Xanthomonas euvesicatoria* / *Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria*)
reference: ICAR Package of Practices for Vegetable Crops; TNAU Plant Pathology Crop Protection Compendium
heading: Favorable Environmental Conditions
content: Warm temperatures (25°C to 30°C) combined with high relative humidity (>85%) and frequent rainfall, overhead irrigation, or heavy dew favor rapid pathogen spread. Splashing water facilitates leaf-to-leaf dissemination.

title: Bacterial Spot of Bell Pepper (Capsicum)
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Horticultural Research (IIHR), Bengaluru & TNAU Agritech Portal
disease: Bacterial Spot (*Xanthomonas euvesicatoria* / *Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria*)
reference: ICAR Package of Practices for Vegetable Crops; TNAU Plant Pathology Crop Protection Compendium
heading: Cultural & Biological Management
content:
1. Use certified disease-free seeds and disease-free nursery seedlings.
2. Hot water seed treatment at 50°C for 25 minutes to eliminate seed-borne inoculum.
3. Adopt drip irrigation rather than overhead sprinklers to keep foliage dry.
4. Practice 2 to 3 years crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops (e.g., maize, pulses).
5. Remove and safely destroy all crop residues after harvest.
6. Spray biological antagonist *Pseudomonas fluorescens* (2 g/L) or *Bacillus subtilis* (2 g/L) at nursery stage and early vegetative growth.

title: Bacterial Spot of Bell Pepper (Capsicum)
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Horticultural Research (IIHR), Bengaluru & TNAU Agritech Portal
disease: Bacterial Spot (*Xanthomonas euvesicatoria* / *Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria*)
reference: ICAR Package of Practices for Vegetable Crops; TNAU Plant Pathology Crop Protection Compendium
heading: Recommended Chemical Management
content:
1. Copper hydroxide 77% WP @ 2.0 g/L or Copper oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5–3.0 g/L.
2. Streptocycline (Streptomycin sulphate + Tetracycline hydrochloride) @ 100 ppm (1 g per 10 litres of water) tank-mixed with copper oxychloride at early appearance of symptoms.
3. Repeat spray at 10 to 14 day intervals depending on weather and disease pressure.

title: Bacterial Spot of Bell Pepper (Capsicum)
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Horticultural Research (IIHR), Bengaluru & TNAU Agritech Portal
disease: Bacterial Spot (*Xanthomonas euvesicatoria* / *Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria*)
reference: ICAR Package of Practices for Vegetable Crops; TNAU Plant Pathology Crop Protection Compendium
heading: Precautions & Withholding Period
content: Avoid excessive copper accumulation in sandy soils. Do not spray during peak noon heat to prevent phytotoxicity. Observe a minimum withholding period of 3 days before harvesting fruits.

title: Good Agricultural Practices for Healthy Bell Pepper
source: ICAR - National Research Centre for Integrated Pest Management (NCIPM), New Delhi
disease: Healthy Foliage, Nutrient Balance, and Preventative IPM
reference: ICAR IPM Guidelines for Horticultural Crops
heading: Characteristics of Healthy Foliage
content: Healthy bell pepper leaves are uniformly deep green, turgid, and free of chlorotic speckles, necrotic spots, or upward cupping. Stems are sturdy and erect with active vegetative apex growth.

title: Good Agricultural Practices for Healthy Bell Pepper
source: ICAR - National Research Centre for Integrated Pest Management (NCIPM), New Delhi
disease: Healthy Foliage, Nutrient Balance, and Preventative IPM
reference: ICAR IPM Guidelines for Horticultural Crops
heading: Soil & Nutrient Management
content:
1. Well-drained sandy loam or clay loam soil with pH 6.0 to 7.0 is ideal.
2. Incorporate well-decomposed Farmyard Manure (FYM) or compost @ 20–25 tonnes/ha during final land preparation.
3. Apply balanced N:P:K fertilizers based on soil test recommendations (typically 120:60:60 kg/ha in split doses).
4. Micronutrient foliar application: Spray 0.2% Zinc sulphate and 0.1% Borax at flower initiation stage to avoid blossom-end rot and leaf distortion.

title: Good Agricultural Practices for Healthy Bell Pepper
source: ICAR - National Research Centre for Integrated Pest Management (NCIPM), New Delhi
disease: Healthy Foliage, Nutrient Balance, and Preventative IPM
reference: ICAR IPM Guidelines for Horticultural Crops
heading: Water & Canopy Management
content:
1. Regulate moisture evenly using drip lines; avoid water-logging at all costs.
2. Maintain adequate spacing (60 cm x 45 cm) to promote airflow and minimize microclimatic humidity in the inner canopy.
3. Mulch with silver-black polyethylene (25–30 micron) or organic straw to suppress weed competition and soil splashing.

title: Good Agricultural Practices for Healthy Bell Pepper
source: ICAR - National Research Centre for Integrated Pest Management (NCIPM), New Delhi
disease: Healthy Foliage, Nutrient Balance, and Preventative IPM
reference: ICAR IPM Guidelines for Horticultural Crops
heading: Preventative Pest & Disease Monitoring
content:
1. Install yellow and blue sticky traps (10–12 traps/acre) to monitor whiteflies, thrips, and aphids early.
2. Spray 0.5% Neem oil (5 ml/L) as a broad-spectrum organic preventive spray every 15 days.
3. Regularly inspect lower leaf surfaces for initial signs of pests or lesions.

title: Potato Early Blight Management
source: ICAR - Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI), Shimla
reference: ICAR-CPRI Technical Bulletin No. 92, Potato Pathology Guide
heading: Symptoms
content: Initial symptoms appear on older lower leaves as small, dry, brown to dark brown necrotic spots. Over time, these spots enlarge and exhibit characteristic concentric rings or "target board" (target spot) patterns bounded by leaf veins. Surrounding leaf tissue typically turns chlorotic (yellow). Under severe infestation, the foliage dries up, droops, and premature defoliation occurs, drastically reducing tuber yield and size.

title: Potato Early Blight Management
source: ICAR - Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI), Shimla
reference: ICAR-CPRI Technical Bulletin No. 92, Potato Pathology Guide
heading: Favorable Environmental Conditions
content: Alternating wet and dry periods with temperatures ranging between 22°C and 28°C and relative humidity around 80% favor pathogen sporulation and infection. Stressed or nitrogen-deficient crops are especially susceptible.

title: Potato Early Blight Management
source: ICAR - Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI), Shimla
reference: ICAR-CPRI Technical Bulletin No. 92, Potato Pathology Guide
heading: Cultural & Preventative Practices
content:
1. Plant certified, disease-free seed tubers.
2. Maintain vigorous crop growth through balanced nitrogen and potassium fertilization. Avoid excess moisture stress.
3. Crop rotation with non-host crops (maize, sorghum, sugarcane) for at least 2 seasons.
4. Destruction of crop debris and infected haulms immediately after tuber harvest.
5. Provide furrow irrigation or drip irrigation; avoid overhead sprinkler wetting of foliage late in the day.

title: Potato Early Blight Management
source: ICAR - Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI), Shimla
reference: ICAR-CPRI Technical Bulletin No. 92, Potato Pathology Guide
heading: Recommended Chemical & Fungicidal Management
content:
1. Prophylactic protective spray: Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.0–2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L.
2. Curative systemic spray (upon symptom manifestation):
   - Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 ml/L, OR
   - Tebuconazole 50% + Trifloxystrobin 25% WG @ 0.6–0.7 g/L, OR
   - Mancozeb + Metalaxyl @ 2.5 g/L.
3. Repeat spray after 10–12 days if warm and humid weather persists.

title: Potato Early Blight Management
source: ICAR - Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI), Shimla
reference: ICAR-CPRI Technical Bulletin No. 92, Potato Pathology Guide
heading: Precautions
content: Rotate fungicides from different chemical groups (FRAC codes) to prevent fungicide resistance in *Alternaria solani*.

title: Potato Late Blight Management
source: ICAR - Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI), Shimla
reference: CPRI Advisory on Potato Blight Forecasting and Management
heading: Symptoms
content: Water-soaked, irregular, light-green to pale spots develop on the tips and margins of lower leaves. In cool, humid weather, these rapidly enlarge into large, dark-brown or purplish-black necrotic lesions. A distinct delicate white mildew (cottony fungal growth/sporangiophores) develops on the lower surface of the leaf encircling the lesion margins, particularly in early morning dew. The disease quickly travels down stems and petioles causing vine collapse with a foul rotting odor.

title: Potato Late Blight Management
source: ICAR - Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI), Shimla
reference: CPRI Advisory on Potato Blight Forecasting and Management
heading: Favorable Environmental Conditions
content: Cool temperatures (12°C to 20°C) with prolonged high relative humidity (>90%) and continuous cloud cover, fog, or intermittent drizzle create epidemic conditions. The disease can decimate an entire field within 7 to 10 days if left untreated.

title: Potato Late Blight Management
source: ICAR - Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI), Shimla
reference: CPRI Advisory on Potato Blight Forecasting and Management
heading: Preventative & Cultural Control
content:
1. Plant certified resistant or tolerant potato varieties (e.g., Kufri Girdhari, Kufri Khyati, Kufri Mohan where adapted).
2. Use healthy seed tubers from certified disease-free cold storage sources.
3. Prophylactic earthing-up to prevent sporangia from washing down into the tuber zone.
4. Haulm cutting (dehaulming) 10–12 days prior to harvesting to prevent tuber infection during digging.

title: Potato Late Blight Management
source: ICAR - Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI), Shimla
reference: CPRI Advisory on Potato Blight Forecasting and Management
heading: Chemical Control Schedule (CPRI Strategy)
content:
1. **Prophylactic (Preventive) Phase**:
   - Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Propineb 70% WP @ 2.5 g/L as soon as weather forecast predicts cool, overcast, and humid conditions before any disease appears.
2. **Curative / Systemic Phase (When first blight lesions appear)**:
   - Cymoxanil 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 3.0 g/L, OR
   - Dimethomorph 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L tank-mixed with Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L, OR
   - Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP (Ridomil MZ) @ 2.5 g/L, OR
   - Mandipropamid 23.4% SC @ 0.8 ml/L.
3. Ensure thorough coverage of both upper and lower leaf canopy surfaces. Reapply after 7–10 days if humid conditions persist.

title: Potato Late Blight Management
source: ICAR - Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI), Shimla
reference: CPRI Advisory on Potato Blight Forecasting and Management
heading: Safety & Post-Harvest Precautions
content: Do not harvest tubers from fields where live blight remains on foliage. Sort and discard any blighted tubers before cold storage to avoid secondary soft rot.

title: Bell Pepper Soil Requirements, Salinity Sensitivity and Drainage
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi & TNAU
disease: Capsicum Soil Aeration, Salinity Tolerance and Micronutrients
reference: TNAU Agritech Portal & Commercial Capsicum Production Manual
heading: Soil Aeration, Drainage and Texture
content:
Bell pepper (Capsicum) has a fibrous and relatively shallow root system (70% of active feeding roots are in the upper 20-30 cm soil layer).
- Optimal Soil Type: Highly well-drained sandy loam, rich loam, or light clay loam with high organic matter (>1.0%).
- Intolerance to Waterlogging: Capsicum is one of the most sensitive horticultural crops to poor soil aeration. Anaerobic soil conditions for even 12 hours cause leaf epinasty (downward leaf curling), flower drop, and rapid outbreak of Phytophthora root and crown rot (*Phytophthora capsici*).
- Raised Bed & Mulching: Planting on 20 cm high raised beds with silver-black polyethylene mulch regulates root-zone soil temperature, prevents weed competition, and maintains uniform soil moisture.

title: Bell Pepper Soil Requirements, Salinity Sensitivity and Drainage
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi & TNAU
disease: Capsicum Soil Aeration, Salinity Tolerance and Micronutrients
reference: TNAU Agritech Portal & Commercial Capsicum Production Manual
heading: Salinity Sensitivity and pH Requirements
content:
- Ideal pH Range: 6.0 to 6.8.
- Salinity Hazard: Bell pepper is classified as moderately sensitive to soil salinity. Electrical Conductivity (EC) of saturation extract exceeding 1.5 dS/m leads to yield reduction of up to 25%, stunted canopy growth, and blossom end rot. In saline soils or with brackish irrigation water, frequent light irrigations and leaching fractions are necessary.

title: Bell Pepper Soil Requirements, Salinity Sensitivity and Drainage
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi & TNAU
disease: Capsicum Soil Aeration, Salinity Tolerance and Micronutrients
reference: TNAU Agritech Portal & Commercial Capsicum Production Manual
heading: Organic Manuring and Micronutrient Balance
content:
- Soil-borne Disease Suppression: Incorporation of 250-500 kg/ha of neem cake into planting beds effectively suppresses plant-parasitic nematodes (*Meloidogyne incognita*) and provides slow-release nitrogen.
- Micronutrient Balance: In high pH or calcareous soils, bell pepper frequently exhibits zinc deficiency (little leaf, rosetting) and iron chlorosis (interveinal yellowing of youngest leaves). Basal soil application of zinc sulphate (20-25 kg/ha) or foliar application of chelated zinc (1.0 g/L) and ferrous sulphate (2.0 g/L with citric acid) prevents physiological deficiencies.

title: Soil Health and Land Resource Management in Indian Agriculture
source: ICAR - National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use Planning (NBSS&LUP), Nagpur & ICAR-CRIDA, Hyderabad
disease: Soil Health, Soil Orders, pH and Nutrient Dynamics
reference: ICAR Benchmark Soils of India & National Soil Health Card Guidelines
heading: Soil Orders and Regional Characteristics
content:
Indian agricultural soils are primarily classified into major orders:
1. Vertisols and Vertic Inceptisols (Black Cotton Soils): Prevalent across Maharashtra (Deccan basaltic plateau), Madhya Pradesh, and Gujarat. High clay content (>40%, predominantly smectite/montmorillonite), high swelling and shrinking characteristics, deep crack formation during dry periods, high moisture holding capacity, and moderate to high cation exchange capacity (CEC 35-55 cmol(c)/kg). Typical pH is neutral to moderately alkaline (7.5 - 8.4).
2. Inceptisols and Entisols (Alluvial and Medium Black Soils): Widespread in river valleys and transitional plains. Variable texture from sandy loam to clay loam, good drainage, moderate fertility, and pH ranging from 6.5 to 7.8.
3. Alfisols and Ultisols (Red and Lateritic Soils): Common in Western Ghats, Konkan coastal strip, and plateau fringes. Coarse to medium textured, prone to acidity (pH 5.0 - 6.5), low water holding capacity, and high phosphorus fixation due to iron and aluminum oxides.

title: Soil Health and Land Resource Management in Indian Agriculture
source: ICAR - National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use Planning (NBSS&LUP), Nagpur & ICAR-CRIDA, Hyderabad
disease: Soil Health, Soil Orders, pH and Nutrient Dynamics
reference: ICAR Benchmark Soils of India & National Soil Health Card Guidelines
heading: Soil Reaction pH and Correction Protocols
content:
Soil pH controls the chemical bioavailability of essential plant macro and micro-nutrients:
- Strongly Acidic (pH < 5.5): Severe phosphorus fixation, aluminum/manganese toxicity, and reduced calcium/magnesium availability. Remediation requires agricultural lime (calcium carbonate CaCO3) or dolomite application at 1.5 to 3.0 tonnes/ha based on soil buffer capacity, incorporated 3-4 weeks prior to transplanting.
- Optimal Neutral (pH 6.2 - 7.2): Maximum nutrient availability for microbial nitrogen fixation, soluble phosphorus, and balanced cation uptake.
- Moderately Alkaline / Calcareous (pH 7.8 - 8.5): Common in Deccan Vertisols. High free calcium carbonate causes fixation of phosphorus (into insoluble calcium phosphates) and micronutrient deficiencies (iron chlorosis, zinc deficiency). Remediation includes regular addition of organic amendments (FYM, compost), sulphur application (150-250 kg/ha), gypsum for sodic conditions, and foliar feeding of chelated micronutrients (Fe-EDTA, Zn-EDTA).

title: Soil Health and Land Resource Management in Indian Agriculture
source: ICAR - National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use Planning (NBSS&LUP), Nagpur & ICAR-CRIDA, Hyderabad
disease: Soil Health, Soil Orders, pH and Nutrient Dynamics
reference: ICAR Benchmark Soils of India & National Soil Health Card Guidelines
heading: Soil Organic Carbon and Biological Fertility
content:
Soil Organic Carbon (SOC) is the primary driver of soil biological activity, aggregate stability, and moisture retention:
- Low SOC (<0.50%): Common in semi-arid tropical soils due to rapid microbial oxidation under high temperatures. Indicates poor microbial biodiversity and low nutrient buffer capacity.
- Medium SOC (0.50% - 0.75%): Moderate fertility requiring maintenance.
- High SOC (>0.75%): Desirable biological fertility.
Recommended Management Practices:
1. Basal incorporation of well-decomposed Farmyard Manure (FYM) or compost at 10-15 tonnes/ha or vermicompost at 2.5-5 tonnes/ha before sowing.
2. In-situ green manuring with Sunnhemp (*Crotalaria juncea*) or Dhaincha (*Sesbania aculeata*) incorporated at 45-50 days (flowering stage), adding 15-20 tonnes/ha of biomass and 60-80 kg N/ha.
3. Inoculation with bio-fertilizers: Azotobacter / Azospirillum for non-symbiotic nitrogen fixation, and Phosphate Solubilizing Bacteria (PSB - *Bacillus megaterium* or *Pseudomonas striata*) at 5 kg/ha mixed with FYM.

title: Soil Health and Land Resource Management in Indian Agriculture
source: ICAR - National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use Planning (NBSS&LUP), Nagpur & ICAR-CRIDA, Hyderabad
disease: Soil Health, Soil Orders, pH and Nutrient Dynamics
reference: ICAR Benchmark Soils of India & National Soil Health Card Guidelines
heading: Macronutrient Indices and Laboratory Soil Testing
content:
Official Indian Soil Health Card critical nutrient limits:
- Available Nitrogen (Alkaline Permanganate method): Low (<280 kg/ha), Medium (280 - 560 kg/ha), High (>560 kg/ha).
- Available Phosphorus (Olsen method for neutral/alkaline soils): Low (<10 kg P/ha or <23 kg P2O5/ha), Medium (10 - 25 kg P/ha), High (>25 kg P/ha).
- Available Potassium (Neutral Ammonium Acetate method): Low (<110 kg K/ha or <133 kg K2O/ha), Medium (110 - 280 kg K/ha), High (>280 kg K2O/ha).
- Salinity Hazard (Electrical Conductivity 1:2 soil-water extract): Non-saline (<1.0 dS/m), Slightly saline / sensitive crop injury (1.0 - 2.0 dS/m), Severely saline (>4.0 dS/m).
Farmers must have a representative composite field soil sample tested at an authorized Soil Testing Laboratory (STL) or Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) every 2-3 years to establish exact field fertilizer schedules.

title: Potato Soil Management, Acidic Preference and Tuberization
source: ICAR - Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI), Shimla
disease: Potato Soil Requirements, Compaction and Common Scab Prevention
reference: CPRI Agronomic Guidelines for Commercial Potato Cultivation
heading: Optimal Soil Physical Conditions and pH Range
content:
Potato is a subterranean tuber crop requiring a loose, friable, well-aerated sandy loam, silt loam, or light alluvial soil with high organic matter content.
- Ideal pH Range: 5.2 to 6.4 (moderately acidic to slightly acidic).
- Common Scab (*Streptomyces scabies*) Warning: Alkaline or limed soils (pH > 6.8 - 7.5) significantly increase the incidence of Common Scab, which causes rough corky lesions on tuber skins. In alkaline soils, avoid liming and use physiologically acidic fertilizers such as ammonium sulphate or apply elemental sulphur.
- Bulk Density and Compaction: Potato roots and stolons cannot penetrate dense or compacted soil layers. Bulk density should remain below 1.35 g/cm³. Hardpan formation causes distorted, irregular, knobby tubers and drastically reduces commercial marketable grade. Deep summer subsoiling followed by fine tilth preparation is essential.

title: Potato Soil Management, Acidic Preference and Tuberization
source: ICAR - Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI), Shimla
disease: Potato Soil Requirements, Compaction and Common Scab Prevention
reference: CPRI Agronomic Guidelines for Commercial Potato Cultivation
heading: Tuber Bulking and Soil Moisture Regulation
content:
Soil moisture within the 0 to 30 cm tuber zone governs tuber initiation and expansion:
- Optimal moisture regime: 65% to 75% of field capacity throughout tuber initiation (20-35 days after planting) and tuber bulking (35-70 days after planting).
- Uneven irrigation (drought followed by heavy irrigation) causes growth cracks, hollow heart, and secondary knobby tuber growth.
- Stagnant water or saturated soil during tuber development restricts gas exchange, promotes lenticel proliferation, and causes soft rot (*Pectobacterium carotovorum*) in the field and storage.

title: Potato Soil Management, Acidic Preference and Tuberization
source: ICAR - Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI), Shimla
disease: Potato Soil Requirements, Compaction and Common Scab Prevention
reference: CPRI Agronomic Guidelines for Commercial Potato Cultivation
heading: Fertilizer Dynamics and Potassium Nutrition
content:
Potato is an exhaustive, heavy consumer of soil nutrients:
- Potassium: Highest nutrient uptake. Potassium Sulphate (SOP - 0-0-50) is strongly preferred over Muriate of Potash (MOP - 0-0-60) because chloride ions reduce tuber starch content, specific gravity, and processing chip quality.
- Organic Matter: Responds dramatically to green manuring or 25 tonnes/ha of well-rotted FYM. Bio-fertilizer treatment of seed tubers with Azotobacter and PSB enhances nutrient uptake efficiency.

title: Tomato Soil Health, Nutrition and Rhizosphere Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Horticultural Research (IIHR), Bengaluru & TNAU Agritech Portal
disease: Tomato Soil Requirements, Salinity and Calcium Nutrition
reference: ICAR Package of Practices for Tomato Production & Plant Nutrition
heading: Optimal Soil Type and Reaction
content:
Tomato thrives in deep, fertile, well-drained loams, sandy loams, or medium black soils rich in organic matter.
- Ideal pH range: 6.0 to 7.0. Tomatoes tolerate mild acidity down to pH 5.5 and mild alkalinity up to pH 7.8.
- Soil Drainage: Tomato roots are extremely sensitive to poor drainage and waterlogging. Subsurface saturation (>24 hours) causes rapid root asphyxiation, wilting, and triggers soil-borne fungal pathogens (*Fusarium oxysporum*, *Pythium*, and *Phytophthora*).
- Raised bed cultivation (15-20 cm height, 90-120 cm width) with drip lateral lines is strongly recommended on heavy black soils (Vertisols) to maintain optimal soil aeration and prevent root diseases.

title: Tomato Soil Health, Nutrition and Rhizosphere Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Horticultural Research (IIHR), Bengaluru & TNAU Agritech Portal
disease: Tomato Soil Requirements, Salinity and Calcium Nutrition
reference: ICAR Package of Practices for Tomato Production & Plant Nutrition
heading: Blossom End Rot and Calcium Moisture Interaction
content:
Blossom End Rot (BER) is a physiological disorder characterized by water-soaked, sunken, leathery black spots at the blossom end of green or ripening tomato fruits.
- Primary Cause: Calcium deficiency in rapidly expanding fruit tissue. This is almost never caused by a simple lack of soil calcium, but rather by fluctuating soil moisture (alternating cycles of drought stress and excessive irrigation) or high soil salinity/EC, which impairs calcium transpirational pull through xylem vessels.
- Management: Maintain consistent root-zone moisture (soil moisture tension 20-30 kPa). Apply agricultural gypsum (calcium sulphate) at 250-500 kg/ha in calcareous or calcium-depleted soils. Apply foliar sprays of calcium nitrate (0.5%) or chelated calcium (0.2%) at flowering and early fruit development stages.

title: Tomato Soil Health, Nutrition and Rhizosphere Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Horticultural Research (IIHR), Bengaluru & TNAU Agritech Portal
disease: Tomato Soil Requirements, Salinity and Calcium Nutrition
reference: ICAR Package of Practices for Tomato Production & Plant Nutrition
heading: Balanced Fertigation and Nutrient Partitioning
content:
Nutrient requirements of tomato vary across physiological stages:
1. Basal Stage: 25-30% of total N, 100% of P (as single superphosphate SSP or DAP), and 25% of K incorporated with organic manure. High phosphorus is critical for early root development.
2. Vegetative to Flowering Stage: Balanced N and K application. Avoid excess nitrogen which promotes excessive succulent foliage, delayed flowering, and vulnerability to suckling pests (whiteflies, aphids) and Early Blight.
3. Fruit Bulking and Harvesting Stage: Heavy potassium demand. Potassium promotes fruit firmness, uniform red pigmentation (lycopene synthesis), total soluble solids (Brix), and shelf life. Apply water-soluble potassium nitrate (13-0-45) or sulphate of potash (0-0-50) via drip fertigation.

title: Tomato Bacterial Spot Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi
disease: Bacterial Spot (*Xanthomonas perforans* / *Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria*)
reference: IIVR Technical Bulletin: Integrated Disease Management in Tomato
heading: Symptoms
content: Small, circular to angular, dark brown to black water-soaked lesions appear on leaves, stems, and pedicels. Lesions often become surrounded by a narrow yellow chlorotic halo. Under high disease pressure, spots coalesce causing leaf blighting, yellowing, and severe defoliation that exposes developing fruit to sunscald. On green fruits, small, slightly raised black blisters emerge which later become scab-like with rough brown centers.

title: Tomato Bacterial Spot Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi
disease: Bacterial Spot (*Xanthomonas perforans* / *Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria*)
reference: IIVR Technical Bulletin: Integrated Disease Management in Tomato
heading: Favorable Environmental Conditions
content: High temperatures (24°C to 30°C) with prolonged relative humidity (>85%) and wind-driven rain or overhead irrigation. The bacterium enters leaves through natural openings (stomata, hydathodes) and microscopic wounds.

title: Tomato Bacterial Spot Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi
disease: Bacterial Spot (*Xanthomonas perforans* / *Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria*)
reference: IIVR Technical Bulletin: Integrated Disease Management in Tomato
heading: Cultural & Preventative Management
content:
1. Use certified disease-free seeds. Treat seeds with hot water at 50°C for 25 minutes or soak in 0.5% sodium hypochlorite for 1 minute before sowing.
2. Space plants adequately (75 cm x 60 cm) and stake tomato vines to improve canopy ventilation and accelerate leaf drying.
3. Strict drip irrigation practice to prevent water splash dissemination.
4. Rotate with non-solanaceous crops such as cereals, legumes, or brassicas for 2–3 seasons.
5. Apply *Pseudomonas fluorescens* (5 g/L) or *Bacillus subtilis* foliar sprays at transplanting and early vegetative stage.

title: Tomato Bacterial Spot Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi
disease: Bacterial Spot (*Xanthomonas perforans* / *Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria*)
reference: IIVR Technical Bulletin: Integrated Disease Management in Tomato
heading: Recommended Chemical Control
content:
1. Spray Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5–3.0 g/L or Copper Hydroxide 77% WP @ 2.0 g/L.
2. Tank mix Copper Oxychloride with Streptocycline (Streptomycin sulphate + Tetracycline hydrochloride) @ 100 ppm (1 g per 10 L water).
3. Re-spray at 10-day intervals if warm, cloudy, and wet weather persists.

title: Tomato Bacterial Spot Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi
disease: Bacterial Spot (*Xanthomonas perforans* / *Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria*)
reference: IIVR Technical Bulletin: Integrated Disease Management in Tomato
heading: Withholding Period & Safety
content: Avoid spraying during active pollination hours. Wear protective equipment and respect a 5-day pre-harvest interval after copper application.

title: Tomato Early Blight Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi & MPKV Rahuri
reference: ICAR Package of Practices for Vegetable Crops
heading: Symptoms
content: Initial infection begins on older, low-lying leaves as dark brown to black circular or irregular necrotic spots. As the lesions expand, characteristic concentric rings develop resembling a miniature bullseye or target pattern, frequently surrounded by a chlorotic yellow zone. Progressive infection causes collar rot at the stem base and dark sunken leathery lesions at the fruit stem attachment end. Infected leaves dry up and shed prematurely.

title: Tomato Early Blight Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi & MPKV Rahuri
reference: ICAR Package of Practices for Vegetable Crops
heading: Favorable Environmental Conditions
content: Moderate to warm temperatures (24°C to 29°C) combined with alternating periods of high humidity (heavy dew or rain) and sunny dry intervals. Stressed, senescent, or poorly fertilized plants are especially prone to infection.

title: Tomato Early Blight Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi & MPKV Rahuri
reference: ICAR Package of Practices for Vegetable Crops
heading: Cultural Practices & IPM
content:
1. Crop rotation: Never follow tomato immediately after potato, eggplant, or capsicum. Rotate with corn, okra, or pulses for 2 years.
2. Staking and mulching: Staking plants off the ground and applying black mulch prevents soil-borne fungal spores from splashing onto lower leaves.
3. Pruning lower leaves: Remove bottom foliage up to 20 cm from the soil once fruit begins setting to minimize soil-leaf contact.
4. Balanced nutrition: Avoid nitrogen deficiency; top-dress with balanced potassium to fortify plant cell wall defenses.

title: Tomato Early Blight Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi & MPKV Rahuri
reference: ICAR Package of Practices for Vegetable Crops
heading: Recommended Fungicides & Application Schedule
content:
1. **Preventive Stage**:
   - Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L, OR Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L, applied every 10–14 days.
2. **Curative Stage (When lesions are detected)**:
   - Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 ml/L, OR
   - Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 ml/L, OR
   - Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0–1.2 ml/L, OR
   - Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 1.0 g/L.

title: Tomato Early Blight Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi & MPKV Rahuri
reference: ICAR Package of Practices for Vegetable Crops
heading: Safety & Waiting Period
content: Always alternate strobilurin fungicides (FRAC 11) with triazole fungicides (FRAC 3) to prevent fungal resistance. Observe a 3–5 day pre-harvest interval before fruit collection.

title: Good Agricultural Practices for Healthy Tomato Cultivation
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi & TNAU Agritech
disease: Healthy Plant Canopy, Nutrition, and Soil Health
reference: ICAR National Guideline for Protected and Open Field Tomato Production
heading: Visual Indicators of Healthy Tomato Canopy
content: Healthy tomato foliage has robust, dark green leaves without chlorotic mottling, necrosis, curled margins, or stippling. Leaf petioles form strong angular attachments to the central stem. Flowering clusters have bright yellow, well-formed petals, and fruit sets develop uniform green coloration without blossom-end browning.

title: Good Agricultural Practices for Healthy Tomato Cultivation
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi & TNAU Agritech
disease: Healthy Plant Canopy, Nutrition, and Soil Health
reference: ICAR National Guideline for Protected and Open Field Tomato Production
heading: Soil, Land Preparation & Nutrition
content:
1. Optimum soil: Well-aerated sandy loam with pH 6.0–6.8 and good organic matter content.
2. Basal fertilization: Apply 25 tonnes/ha well-rotted Farmyard Manure (FYM) fortified with *Trichoderma viride* (2.5 kg/ha) and *Pseudomonas fluorescens* (2.5 kg/ha) 15 days prior to planting.
3. Mineral nutrition: N:P:K 150:100:100 kg/ha with nitrogen applied in 3 equal splits (at transplanting, 30 days, and 60 days).
4. Micronutrient spray: Apply foliar spray of vegetable micronutrient mixture (containing Zn, B, Fe, Mn) @ 2.5 g/L at flower initiation and fruit enlargement.

title: Good Agricultural Practices for Healthy Tomato Cultivation
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi & TNAU Agritech
disease: Healthy Plant Canopy, Nutrition, and Soil Health
reference: ICAR National Guideline for Protected and Open Field Tomato Production
heading: Irrigation & Microclimate Management
content:
1. Regulate moisture evenly using drip irrigation to avoid fruit cracking and blossom-end rot (caused by erratic water supply and localized calcium deficiency).
2. Staking: Stake indeterminate and semi-determinate tomato varieties using bamboo poles and plastic twine to keep foliage 30 cm above soil level.
3. Aeration: Prune lower auxiliary shoots (suckers) up to the first flower cluster to maintain canopy air circulation and sunlight penetration.

title: Good Agricultural Practices for Healthy Tomato Cultivation
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi & TNAU Agritech
disease: Healthy Plant Canopy, Nutrition, and Soil Health
reference: ICAR National Guideline for Protected and Open Field Tomato Production
heading: Preventative IPM Measures
content:
1. Install yellow sticky traps (10–12 traps/acre) for whiteflies and pheromone traps (5 traps/acre) for tomato fruit borer (*Helicoverpa armigera*).
2. Spray 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE) or 0.3% Neem oil (3 ml/L) as a prophylactic pest deterrent every 15 days.
3. Monitor the field twice a week for early signs of disease or nutrient deficiency.

title: Tomato Late Blight Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR) & Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI)
reference: ICAR Plant Protection Bulletin: Oomycete Disease Management
heading: Symptoms
content: Large, irregular, pale-green to water-soaked dark brown or purplish-black lesions appear abruptly on leaves and petioles. Under cool, humid mornings, a delicate downy white mold (sporulation) appears on the abaxial (lower) surface of infected leaves along the lesion perimeter. Stems develop dark brown greasy lesions leading to branch collapse. Developing green fruits display greasy, olive-brown to bronze, firm water-soaked lesions that cause fruit rot.

title: Tomato Late Blight Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR) & Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI)
reference: ICAR Plant Protection Bulletin: Oomycete Disease Management
heading: Favorable Environmental Conditions
content: Cool temperatures (15°C to 22°C) with persistent high relative humidity (>90%), dense fog, continuous drizzle, or sustained dew. The disease spreads extremely rapidly via airborne sporangia and can ruin an entire tomato patch within 5 to 7 days.

title: Tomato Late Blight Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR) & Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI)
reference: ICAR Plant Protection Bulletin: Oomycete Disease Management
heading: Preventative Cultural Measures
content:
1. Avoid planting adjacent to potato fields infected with late blight.
2. Space rows generously (at least 90 cm) to maximize air movement through the foliage.
3. Eliminate wild solanaceous weeds (*Solanum nigrum*) around field perimeters.
4. Adopt drip irrigation; do not use overhead irrigation during cool cloudy weather.

title: Tomato Late Blight Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR) & Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI)
reference: ICAR Plant Protection Bulletin: Oomycete Disease Management
heading: Recommended Fungicidal Management
content:
1. **Preventive (Before disease onset when cool wet weather is forecasted)**:
   - Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L, OR
   - Propineb 70% WP @ 2.5 g/L, OR
   - Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L.
2. **Curative / Systemic (At first appearance of water-soaked spots)**:
   - Metalaxyl-M 4% + Mancozeb 64% WP (Ridomil Gold) @ 2.5 g/L, OR
   - Cymoxanil 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 3.0 g/L, OR
   - Dimethomorph 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L combined with Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L, OR
   - Famoxadone 16.6% + Cymoxanil 22.1% SC @ 1.0 ml/L.
3. Repeat spray at 7-day intervals under active disease pressure.

title: Tomato Late Blight Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR) & Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI)
reference: ICAR Plant Protection Bulletin: Oomycete Disease Management
heading: Critical Precautions
content: Do not apply the same systemic fungicide more than twice in succession to forestall fungicide resistance development.

title: Tomato Leaf Mold Management
source: Tamil Nadu Agricultural University (TNAU) Agritech Portal & ICAR
reference: TNAU Crop Protection Compendium for Horticultural Crops
heading: Symptoms
content: Initial symptoms manifest as pale yellow to light green diffuse patches on the upper surface of older leaves. Directly beneath these yellow patches on the lower leaf surface, an olive-green, tan to velvety purplish-brown fungal mold forms. As the fungus sporulates profusely, the yellow spots turn brown, and the entire leaf curls, withers, and prematurely drops off. Blossoms and young fruit stems may abort under severe infections.

title: Tomato Leaf Mold Management
source: Tamil Nadu Agricultural University (TNAU) Agritech Portal & ICAR
reference: TNAU Crop Protection Compendium for Horticultural Crops
heading: Favorable Environmental Conditions
content: Warm temperatures (21°C to 27°C) accompanied by very high relative humidity (>85%). Particularly destructive in protected cultivation (polyhouses, shade net structures) and densely planted, poorly ventilated field stands.

title: Tomato Leaf Mold Management
source: Tamil Nadu Agricultural University (TNAU) Agritech Portal & ICAR
reference: TNAU Crop Protection Compendium for Horticultural Crops
heading: Cultural & Environmental Management
content:
1. Enhance ventilation: Open side curtains in greenhouses and increase row spacing in open fields to decrease leaf wetness duration.
2. Maintain relative humidity below 80% through proper ventilation and avoid overhead misting.
3. Prune suckers and lower senescent leaves to allow sunlight and wind penetration.
4. Hot water seed treatment at 50°C for 25 minutes to eradicate seed-borne fungal spores.

title: Tomato Leaf Mold Management
source: Tamil Nadu Agricultural University (TNAU) Agritech Portal & ICAR
reference: TNAU Crop Protection Compendium for Horticultural Crops
heading: Recommended Fungicidal Control
content:
1. Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Bordeaux Mixture 1.0%.
2. Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective preventative spray.
3. Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 ml/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 ml/L at first sign of velvety sporulation on the underside of leaves.
4. Ensure spray droplets thoroughly wet the underside of the foliage where fungal sporulation occurs.

title: Tomato Leaf Mold Management
source: Tamil Nadu Agricultural University (TNAU) Agritech Portal & ICAR
reference: TNAU Crop Protection Compendium for Horticultural Crops
heading: Precautions
content: Do not apply copper sprays during very cloudy, damp weather when spray dry-time exceeds 3 hours, as leaf burn may occur.

title: Tomato Septoria Leaf Spot Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR) & State Agricultural Universities
reference: ICAR Vegetable Pathology Compendium
heading: Symptoms
content: Numerous tiny, circular spots (1.5 to 3 mm in diameter) appear on older lower leaves. The spots characteristically have dark brown to black borders with pale white or ash-grey centers. Within mature spots, tiny black specks (pycnidia / fungal fruiting bodies) are clearly visible under magnification. Severely affected leaves turn completely yellow, wither, and drop, creating severe upward defoliation that exposes fruits to solar injury and reduces yields.

title: Tomato Septoria Leaf Spot Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR) & State Agricultural Universities
reference: ICAR Vegetable Pathology Compendium
heading: Favorable Environmental Conditions
content: Warm temperatures (20°C to 26°C) combined with high relative humidity and prolonged leaf wetness (longer than 8 hours). Rain splashes or overhead irrigation easily detach and splash spores from infected lower debris onto upper leaves.

title: Tomato Septoria Leaf Spot Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR) & State Agricultural Universities
reference: ICAR Vegetable Pathology Compendium
heading: Cultural & Preventative Practices
content:
1. Crop rotation: Rotate fields away from tomato, potato, or eggplant for 2–3 seasons.
2. Clean cultivation: Remove and destroy tomato plant residue and solanaceous weeds immediately after final harvest.
3. Mulch and stake: Lay plastic or straw mulch and stake plants upright to eliminate contact between bottom leaves and wet soil.
4. Bottom leaf pruning: Strip lower leaves up to 25 cm from the soil line once crown clusters have set.

title: Tomato Septoria Leaf Spot Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR) & State Agricultural Universities
reference: ICAR Vegetable Pathology Compendium
heading: Recommended Fungicidal Control
content:
1. **Preventive Foliar Sprays**:
   - Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L, OR
   - Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L, OR
   - Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L.
2. **Systemic Curative Sprays (At disease onset)**:
   - Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 ml/L, OR
   - Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 1.0 g/L, OR
   - Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 ml/L.
3. Reapply at 10 to 14 day intervals depending on rain frequency.

title: Tomato Septoria Leaf Spot Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR) & State Agricultural Universities
reference: ICAR Vegetable Pathology Compendium
heading: Precautions
content: Avoid walking through wet fields during morning dew or after rain to avoid spreading pycnidiospores on clothing and tools.

title: Two-Spotted Spider Mite Management in Tomato
source: ICAR - National Bureau of Agricultural Insect Resources (NBAIR) & DPPQS
reference: ICAR-NBAIR Pest Management Advisory for Horticultural Crops
heading: Symptoms & Identification
content: Spider mites live on the underside of tomato leaves where they puncture plant cells with their stylets and suck sap. The upper leaf surface displays characteristic fine yellow or white stippling (speckling). As mite populations surge, leaves turn bronzed, leathery, or desiccated, and extensive fine webbing covers leaf surfaces, shoot terminals, and flower clusters. Premature leaf drop and stunted growth result under heavy infestation.

title: Two-Spotted Spider Mite Management in Tomato
source: ICAR - National Bureau of Agricultural Insect Resources (NBAIR) & DPPQS
reference: ICAR-NBAIR Pest Management Advisory for Horticultural Crops
heading: Favorable Environmental Conditions
content: Hot, dry, and dusty weather (temperatures >30°C and relative humidity <50%) accelerates spider mite reproduction; a single generation can complete in just 7 to 10 days. Water stress severely exacerbates mite damage.

title: Two-Spotted Spider Mite Management in Tomato
source: ICAR - National Bureau of Agricultural Insect Resources (NBAIR) & DPPQS
reference: ICAR-NBAIR Pest Management Advisory for Horticultural Crops
heading: Cultural & Biological Control
content:
1. Maintain optimum soil moisture; avoid water stress during hot dry spells.
2. Overhead sprinkler or water jet spraying can dislodge mites and disrupt web-building.
3. Conserve and augment natural predatory mites (e.g., *Neoseiulus californicus*, *Phytoseiulus persimilis*).
4. Spray botanical formulations: Neem oil (Azadirachtin 10,000 ppm) @ 2.0–3.0 ml/L or Pongamia oil @ 5.0 ml/L.
5. Destroy broadleaf weed hosts (*Amaranthus*, *Chenopodium*) around field boundaries.

title: Two-Spotted Spider Mite Management in Tomato
source: ICAR - National Bureau of Agricultural Insect Resources (NBAIR) & DPPQS
reference: ICAR-NBAIR Pest Management Advisory for Horticultural Crops
heading: Recommended Acaricides (Chemical Control)
content:
1. Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 ml/L (highly effective against nymph and egg stages).
2. Propargite 57% EC @ 2.0 ml/L (effective contact adulticide).
3. Fenazaquin 10% EC @ 1.5–2.0 ml/L, OR
4. Abamectin 1.9% EC @ 0.75–1.0 ml/L.
5. Ensure high-pressure spray directed specifically at the undersides of the foliage.

title: Two-Spotted Spider Mite Management in Tomato
source: ICAR - National Bureau of Agricultural Insect Resources (NBAIR) & DPPQS
reference: ICAR-NBAIR Pest Management Advisory for Horticultural Crops
heading: Safety & Waiting Period
content: Do not use broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids (e.g., Cypermethrin) as they eliminate natural predatory mites and cause catastrophic mite flare-ups. Observe a minimum 5-day withholding period before harvest.

title: Tomato Target Spot Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi
reference: ICAR Crop Protection Guide for Solanaceous Crops
heading: Symptoms
content: Target spot produces small, brown, pinpoint spots on foliage that enlarge into circular to irregular lesions with pale brown to tan centers and distinct concentric brown rings (hence "target spot"). Lesions are often surrounded by a prominent yellow chlorotic halo. Severe infections cause extensive premature defoliation starting from the lower canopy upwards. On green fruit, small, slightly sunken circular lesions with light brown centers develop that cause cracking and soft rot.

title: Tomato Target Spot Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi
reference: ICAR Crop Protection Guide for Solanaceous Crops
heading: Favorable Environmental Conditions
content: Warm temperatures (25°C to 32°C) combined with high relative humidity (>80%) and prolonged leaf wetness (longer than 12 hours). Dense canopies with poor ventilation exacerbate disease incidence.

title: Tomato Target Spot Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi
reference: ICAR Crop Protection Guide for Solanaceous Crops
heading: Cultural & Preventative Practices
content:
1. Avoid overhead irrigation and ensure foliage dries quickly after rain.
2. Space rows at 90 cm x 60 cm to allow wind penetration throughout the canopy.
3. Remove old, senescent lower leaves to reduce proximity to soil moisture.
4. Rotate with non-host monocot crops (sorghum, corn, pearl millet) for 2 seasons.

title: Tomato Target Spot Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi
reference: ICAR Crop Protection Guide for Solanaceous Crops
heading: Recommended Fungicides
content:
1. Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective preventative spray.
2. Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 ml/L.
3. Fluxapyroxad + Pyraclostrobin @ 0.6 ml/L.
4. Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L applied every 10 days during cloudy, humid weather.

title: Tomato Target Spot Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi
reference: ICAR Crop Protection Guide for Solanaceous Crops
heading: Precautions
content: Rotate fungicide classes to prevent resistance. Maintain recommended dilution rates to avoid leaf tip burn.

title: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Horticultural Research (IIHR), Bengaluru
reference: IIHR Farmer Advisory on Tomato Virus Management
heading: Symptoms
content: Infected tomato plants show severe stunting, erect bushy growth, and shortened internodes. Leaves become greatly reduced in size, curl upward and inward (cupping), become puckered and crinkled, and show pronounced interveinal chlorosis (yellowing) with pale green margins. Plants infected early in the season remain severely dwarfed and flower blossoms drop off without setting fruit, leading to total yield loss.

title: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Horticultural Research (IIHR), Bengaluru
reference: IIHR Farmer Advisory on Tomato Virus Management
heading: Transmission & Epidemiology
content: TYLCV is not transmitted through seed or mechanical touch; it is persistently transmitted exclusively by the whitefly (*Bemisia tabaci*). Warm, dry weather encourages high whitefly populations and rapid virus dissemination across fields.

title: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Horticultural Research (IIHR), Bengaluru
reference: IIHR Farmer Advisory on Tomato Virus Management
heading: Integrated Vector & Disease Management
content:
1. **Nursery Protection**:
   - Raise tomato nursery under insect-proof net house (40–50 mesh nylon net) to prevent whiteflies from feeding on seedlings before transplanting.
   - Drench seedlings with Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 0.5 ml/L 5 days prior to field transplanting.
2. **Field Management**:
   - Use virus-tolerant/resistant commercial hybrids (e.g., Arka Rakshak, Arka Samrat, US-440).
   - Install yellow sticky traps @ 20–25 traps/acre evenly at canopy height to capture adult whiteflies.
   - Grow 2–3 border rows of tall barrier crops (maize, pearl millet, or sorghum) 20 days prior to transplanting to obstruct whitefly flight.
   - Mulch with reflective silver-colored polyethylene film to repel incoming whiteflies.
3. **Chemical Vector Control (Early Field Stage)**:
   - Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.2 g/L, OR
   - Cyantraniliprole 10.26% OD @ 1.8 ml/L, OR
   - Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 ml/L, OR
   - Acetamiprid 20% SP @ 0.3 g/L.
4. Rogue and burn or bury infected plants immediately upon early symptom detection to reduce local virus reservoir.

title: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) Management
source: ICAR - Indian Institute of Horticultural Research (IIHR), Bengaluru
reference: IIHR Farmer Advisory on Tomato Virus Management
heading: Precautions
content: Insecticides kill the insect vector, not the virus inside the plant. Once a plant is systemically infected with TYLCV, it cannot be cured; prevention and early vector control are paramount.
